name: Avonmouth
title: Avonmouth and Royal Portbury Ship UTM | Bristol Port Gauging
description: Thickness gauging at Avonmouth and Royal Portbury for car carriers, bulk carriers, feeders and tankers: vehicle decks, holds, ballast tanks and piping.
h1: Ship Thickness Measurement at Avonmouth and Royal Portbury Docks
intro: Avonmouth and Royal Portbury make up the Port of Bristol: two enclosed docks either side of the mouth of the River Avon, where the Severn tide is at its most extreme. Car carriers, bulk carriers with animal feed and grain, container feeders and product tankers all spend time behind the locks, and that time can be used to gauge hull, decks and tanks. Atlantis sends technicians from India to board each ship at her berth; nobody of ours is waiting at the port, so every job begins with a written plan.

highlights.p: Royal Portbury is one of Britain's main gateways for imported and exported vehicles, so pure car and truck carriers call constantly. Vehicle decks, hoistable deck panels, ramps and stern door structure wear in ways cargo holds do not, and gauging them suits a long discharge.

Avonmouth Dock and Royal Portbury Dock each have their own lock from the estuary, and Portbury's takes the larger ships. On either bank the agent's lock plan decides when the team can board, and once inside a ship lies in level water for the whole call.

highlights.h: Feed and grain ships discharging slowly
highlights.p: Bulk carriers landing animal feed and grain into dockside stores empty their holds one at a time over several days. That pace leaves room to gauge frames, hopper plating and tank tops in each emptied hold, and to open ballast tanks while the cargo plan keeps the ship stable.

port.h: The Port of Bristol: two locked docks at the mouth of the Avon
p: The River Avon reaches the Severn estuary a few miles downstream of Bristol, and the city's modern port grew up at the river mouth once ships became too large to reach the old city docks. Avonmouth Dock lies on the north bank, and Royal Portbury Dock, opened in the late 1970s, on the south bank. Both are operated by The Bristol Port Company and both are entered through locks, because the estuary outside has a tidal range among the greatest in the world and strong streams sweep across the approaches. Ships embark a pilot out in the Bristol Channel and time their arrival to the lock schedule around high water. The Severn bridges lie just upstream, and the open estuary to the west offers little natural shelter, so weather and tide together decide when ships come and go.

The port handles a broad mix of cargo. Royal Portbury is dominated by vehicles, with large car carriers discharging imports and loading exports, alongside dry bulks such as animal feed, grain and other agricultural products handled through dockside sheds and silos. Avonmouth has a container terminal served by feeder and short-sea services, together with berths for forest products, metals, aggregates and liquid bulks, including fuels held at terminals close to the docks. The resulting fleet is varied: pure car and truck carriers, bulk carriers up to the size the locks allow, container feeders, general cargo ships, product tankers and coasters. Most of these ships are managed far from Bristol and arrive on liner rotations or charter voyages, so the port becomes a fixed point where a superintendent can count on the ship being still for a while.

Time alongside depends on the trade. A car carrier can discharge and load in a day or less, but ships working large numbers of vehicles in both directions, or waiting for a lock, may stay longer. Bulk carriers discharging feed or grain usually remain several days, and container feeders turn round in hours. Because both docks are impounded, the water does not rise or fall during the call and gangways stay steady through every tide. The weather window matters mainly on arrival: in strong westerlies the estuary becomes rough, and ships may wait at anchor in the Bristol Channel before berthing. Launch boarding at that anchorage is rarely practical in a winter blow, so most work is planned for the period inside the dock, with the ship's agent following the lock plan hour by hour.

facilities.h: Berths at Avonmouth and Portbury where gauging fits
p: On car carriers, the team works the vehicle decks that have been cleared, starting with the lower decks and weather-deck areas the cargo plan releases first. Deck plating under lashing points, hoistable panels and their supports, ramp structure and the bottom of the stern ramp opening are common items, together with ballast tanks and engine-room piping. Bulk carriers at the feed and grain berths are handled hold by hold, with every reading tied to a frame number on the ship's own drawings so it can be compared at the next survey.

Neither dock is a repair base for merchant tonnage, so dockings are booked elsewhere, at yards in South Wales, Cornwall, on the Mersey or on the continent. Gauging at Bristol therefore tends to be preparation: a pre-docking estimate, an owner's condition survey before a charter renewal, or a targeted check after a surveyor has flagged a problem. Tankers at the liquid bulk berths are worked under the terminal's permit system and limited to areas that are safe during cargo transfer, while feeder ships get short, prepared scopes fitted to their berth windows.
list: Royal Portbury car terminals — vehicle deck, ramp, hoistable deck and ballast tank gauging on car carriers during discharge and loading.
Portbury bulk berths — hold, hopper and tank top readings on feed and grain carriers as holds are emptied.
Avonmouth container terminal — piping, upper deck and prepared-tank checks on feeders within their berth window.
Avonmouth general cargo and forest-product berths — hold frames, hatch covers and coamings on multipurpose ships.
Liquid bulk berths — deck and pipe-rack measurements on product tankers under terminal permits.
Lay-by berths in either dock — longer condition surveys while a ship waits for cargo or a repair slot.

context.h: Regulation and trade pressures at the Port of Bristol
p: The Maritime and Coastguard Agency carries out port state control at Avonmouth and Royal Portbury, applying the Paris MoU's risk-based targeting under UK law. Car carriers have faced closer scrutiny across the industry since a run of serious fires on vehicle carriers, and the growing number of electric vehicles has added to attention on decks and ventilation. Gauging does not address fire risk directly, but wasted deck plating and corroded ventilation trunking are among the things inspectors and charterers look at. Older bulk carriers in the feed trades face the familiar questions about hold frames and tank tops, especially once the ESP extent grows after the ship's third renewal survey.

Ships calling at UK ports are expected to carry an Inventory of Hazardous Materials under the ship recycling rules the UK retained from EU law, and owners often combine the IHM review with a broader condition check when deciding how long to keep an ageing ship. For car carriers trading between Bristol and continental Europe, the EU Emissions Trading System counts half of the emissions on each voyage to or from an EU port, one more reason owners are weighing the remaining life of older tonnage against newer, more efficient ships. A clear record of steel condition makes that decision far easier to take.

jobs.h: Common thickness gauging jobs at Avonmouth and Portbury
jobs.p: Jobs at Bristol are usually built around a long discharge. A superintendent tells us which survey is coming, the agent confirms the berth and the hours the ship expects to be inside, and the team takes each deck or hold as it is released. Car carriers and bulk carriers produce most of the work, while tankers and feeders tend to need short, focused scopes. Where a ship returns on a regular rotation, as many car carriers do, a large programme can be split across two or three calls so that no single call is overloaded and the crew can prepare spaces in turn.
list: Vehicle deck and ramp gauging on a pure car and truck carrier approaching its second renewal survey, divided over two rotations.
ESP preparation on a bulk carrier discharging feed at Portbury, with hold frames, hopper plating and ballast tanks gauged as holds empty.
Owner's condition survey of a container feeder covering engine-room and ballast piping, deck and prepared tanks within the berth window.
Pre-purchase gauging of a general cargo ship lying at Avonmouth between charters.
Scrubber wash-water and overboard piping UT on a car carrier fitted with an exhaust gas cleaning system.

logistics: Bristol Airport handles European connections, while long-haul arrivals from India come through London Heathrow and continue by rail to Bristol Parkway or Bristol Temple Meads, then by road to the docks on either bank. The team travels on UK visas, so a first visit needs several weeks of notice. Both docks are ISPS-controlled: the ship's agent requests gate passes in advance, confirms the berth and lock times and, where a terminal runs its own induction, books it before the team arrives.

faqs.q: Can vehicle decks be gauged while a car carrier is discharging at Royal Portbury?
faqs.a: Yes, deck by deck as they are cleared. Stevedores drive vehicles off in a set order, and the team follows on the decks the chief officer releases, measuring plating, lashing-point areas, hoistable panel supports and ramp structure. On a short call the scope is prioritised with the superintendent; on a ship that returns regularly, the decks can be shared across several calls.

faqs.q: Is Avonmouth or Royal Portbury better for a long gauging programme?
faqs.a: It depends on the cargo rather than the dock. Feed and grain carriers at Portbury and general cargo ships at Avonmouth tend to stay longest, which suits full tank and hold programmes, whereas container feeders at Avonmouth turn round quickly. Both docks are impounded, so once inside, a ship lies in level water and the work is never interrupted by the tide outside.

faqs.q: Can a ship be gauged at anchor in the Bristol Channel before berthing?
faqs.a: Only occasionally. The estuary has strong streams and little shelter, and launch boarding is often unsafe in the westerly weather that typically delays ships. If the forecast is calm and the agent can arrange a launch, a short deck scope is possible, but we plan the real work for after the ship is alongside inside the locks and her crew have time to prepare spaces.

faqs.q: Where do ships trading to Bristol go for drydocking?
faqs.a: To a repair yard elsewhere, chosen for size and availability, with South Wales, Cornwall, the Mersey and continental yards all common choices. Gauging at Avonmouth or Portbury in the weeks before the docking means the yard receives a steel list in advance, plate can be ordered early, and staging can be planned before the ship comes in.
